claims.text: The Cr-free Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Dendritic/interdendritic micro-segregation produces asymmetric XRD peaks in the Cr-free alloy.
The Cr-free alloy has low room-temperature fracture strain because micro-segregation creates stress concentrations.
Adding approximately 4 at.% Cr exceeds the solubility limit of Cr in the BCC matrix.
Cr addition drives precipitation of a complex multicomponent C14 or C15 Laves phase.
The Cr-induced Laves phase occupies approximately 4 vol.%, with the operative boundary specified as 3–5 vol.%.
The Laves phase precipitates preferentially at interdendritic boundaries.
The Laves phase forms a continuous reticulated or interconnected network.
The interconnected Laves network is brittle and provides a continuous path for crack propagation.
The Laves network bypasses crack-bridging and crack-deflection mechanisms.
A portion of the added Cr remains dissolved in the BCC matrix.
Cr has a smaller atomic radius than Hf, Zr, and Ti.
Dissolved Cr causes lattice distortion and a net contraction of the BCC lattice parameter.
Cr-induced lattice distortion produces solid-solution hardening and increases yield strength.
Solid-solution hardening from Cr reduces strain-hardening capacity and promotes premature fracture.
The Cr-containing alloy will retain or further decrease its fracture strain relative to the Cr-free baseline while its yield strength increases.
Lattice contraction will shift the BCC (110) diffraction peak to higher 2θ.
XRD will show weak peaks from the Laves phase.
Fractography will reveal intergranular fracture along the interdendritic Laves network.
Homogenization at 1200°C for 24 hours will facilitate phase separation while retaining the interdendritic network morphology.

contradictions.description: The secondary phase is located at interdendritic boundaries, but the predicted fracture is called intergranular. Interdendritic and grain-boundary paths are not necessarily identical, so the asserted fracture path is internally ambiguous.
